Wahlang Ka  Poitri  n Primrose  Gatphob Na  ka  Hyndai  sha  ka  Lawei (dang  shon) THIS  IS  not  the  first  book  of  literary  criticism  nor  is  it the  first  critical  work  in  Khasi  because  Khasi  literary  criti- cism was  born  as  early  as  192S  much  before  I was  born; however  the  first  work  in  book  form  was  published  only  in 1976  which  was  follow^  by  another  in  1977. Literary  criticism  is  not  “book  review’*,  nor  is  it  a mere “appreciation”  as  Mr. Rymbai  held  it  in  197S. Surely, no  literary  critic  would  be  prepared  to  act  as  advertising agent  of  authors  and  publishets. This  book,  I believe,  will answer  many  of  the  questions  on  the  subject. At  the  time  of  writing,  one  primary  question  engaged my  mind:  should  I cover  all  the  major  literary  critics  or should  I concentrate  only  on  Khasi  critics,  or  should  I look only  for  a point  ? The  course  prescribed  by  the  previous  Board  of  Under- graduate Studies  for  our  Honours  students  is  too  vast  and vague;  The  label  ''History  of  Criticism”  immediately  tells a student  of  that  subject  that  it  covers  from  Plato  down  to F. Leavis,  and  from  the  first  Khasi  critic  down  to  the present  one;  Finally,  I thought  1 was  competent enough  to  decide  which  of  those  critics  to  be  taught  in  the class  and  which  ones  to  be  simply  mentioned. But  why from  Plato  to  Wordsworth  only  ? Why  not  at  least  Cole- ridge, Shelley,  Arnold,  Pater,  FJiot,  Richards  and  Leavis: Some  of  my  class-friends  may  have  such  question  in  mind. 1 left  those,  as  well  as  some  Khasi  critics  for  two  reasons. I have  left  out  in  this  edition  some  major  English  critics because  those  had  not  much  influence  on  Khasi  criticism.

Secondly,  the  course  of  study  as  it  is  now  is  too  limited  for such  a scope  as  the  subject  is  only  a part  of  one  paper  at Honours. On  the  other  hand,  a few  critics  of  English literature  may  wonder  how  Milton  comes  to  have  one  full chapter  in  this  book  when  even  his  fellow  countrymen  have ii not  given  him  a proper  place  in  the  history  of  criticism. The  reason  is  that  Milton  has  a great  deal  of  influence  on our  poets,  therefore,  a critical  history  of  Khasi  criticism would  be  somewhat  incomplete  without  him. This  book  is  not  a plain  history  of  criticism  because much  of  my  own  ciritical  tools  have  been  used  all  through. It  may  give  a senior  literary  historian,  who  at  a certain  place regards  me  as  “a  critic  of  poetry’*,  a new  food  for  thought It  nuy  even  change  bis  ju^ment.'  At  the  same  time  I feel that  my  colleagues  in  the  teaching  profession  and  in  literary pursuit  may,  after  studying  the  last  four  chapters,  decide whether  they  are  still  convinced  that  I "will  be  remembered by  posterity  as  the  real  harbinger  of  literary  criticism”,  as one  of  our  scholars  adjudged  me  in  1978. In  conclusion  I acknowledge  a debt  of  gratitude  to  Dr. Lynsdoh  who  never  failed  to  remind  me  of  the  need  to have  books  on  this  subject  till  be  saw  that  I was  already writing  this;  to  Professor  A.G. George  for  bis  confidence that  the  training  he  gave  us  inside  and  outside  the  "Mayur- bhanj"  was  suffidenl  to  make  us  critics  of  any  literature  we can  read. If  this  book  fails,  it  is  not  for  lack  of  encourage- ment from  them. Garikhana,  Shillong, September  9, 1979i H.W. Sten 1. Wahlang Ka  Poitri  n Primrose  Gatphob Na  ka  Hyndai  sha  ka  Lawei (dang  shon) THIS  IS  not  the  first  book  of  literary  criticism  nor  is  it the  first  critical  work  in  Khasi  because  Khasi  literary  criti- cism was  born  as  early  as  192S  much  before  I was  born; however  the  first  work  in  book  form  was  published  only  in 1976  which  was  follow^  by  another  in  1977. Literary  criticism  is  not  “book  review’*,  nor  is  it  a mere “appreciation”  as  Mr. Rymbai  held  it  in  197S. Surely, no  literary  critic  would  be  prepared  to  act  as  advertising agent  of  authors  and  publishets. This  book,  I believe,  will answer  many  of  the  questions  on  the  subject. At  the  time  of  writing,  one  primary  question  engaged my  mind:  should  I cover  all  the  major  literary  critics  or should  I concentrate  only  on  Khasi  critics,  or  should  I look only  for  a point  ? The  course  prescribed  by  the  previous  Board  of  Under- graduate Studies  for  our  Honours  students  is  too  vast  and vague;  The  label  ''History  of  Criticism”  immediately  tells a student  of  that  subject  that  it  covers  from  Plato  down  to F. Leavis,  and  from  the  first  Khasi  critic  down  to  the present  one;  Finally,  I thought  1 was  competent enough  to  decide  which  of  those  critics  to  be  taught  in  the class  and  which  ones  to  be  simply  mentioned. But  why from  Plato  to  Wordsworth  only  ? Why  not  at  least  Cole- ridge, Shelley,  Arnold,  Pater,  FJiot,  Richards  and  Leavis: Some  of  my  class-friends  may  have  such  question  in  mind. 1 left  those,  as  well  as  some  Khasi  critics  for  two  reasons. I have  left  out  in  this  edition  some  major  English  critics because  those  had  not  much  influence  on  Khasi  criticism.

Secondly,  the  course  of  study  as  it  is  now  is  too  limited  for such  a scope  as  the  subject  is  only  a part  of  one  paper  at Honours. On  the  other  hand,  a few  critics  of  English literature  may  wonder  how  Milton  comes  to  have  one  full chapter  in  this  book  when  even  his  fellow  countrymen  have ii not  given  him  a proper  place  in  the  history  of  criticism. The  reason  is  that  Milton  has  a great  deal  of  influence  on our  poets,  therefore,  a critical  history  of  Khasi  criticism would  be  somewhat  incomplete  without  him. This  book  is  not  a plain  history  of  criticism  because much  of  my  own  ciritical  tools  have  been  used  all  through. It  may  give  a senior  literary  historian,  who  at  a certain  place regards  me  as  “a  critic  of  poetry’*,  a new  food  for  thought It  nuy  even  change  bis  ju^ment.'  At  the  same  time  I feel that  my  colleagues  in  the  teaching  profession  and  in  literary pursuit  may,  after  studying  the  last  four  chapters,  decide whether  they  are  still  convinced  that  I "will  be  remembered by  posterity  as  the  real  harbinger  of  literary  criticism”,  as one  of  our  scholars  adjudged  me  in  1978. In  conclusion  I acknowledge  a debt  of  gratitude  to  Dr. Lynsdoh  who  never  failed  to  remind  me  of  the  need  to have  books  on  this  subject  till  be  saw  that  I was  already writing  this;  to  Professor  A.G. George  for  bis  confidence that  the  training  he  gave  us  inside  and  outside  the  "Mayur- bhanj"  was  suffidenl  to  make  us  critics  of  any  literature  we can  read. If  this  book  fails,  it  is  not  for  lack  of  encourage- ment from  them. Garikhana,  Shillong, September  9, 1979i H.W. Sten 1.
